items.summary: Static application security testing (SAST) tools such as CodeQL serve as security gates in continuous integration and code review, and a gate is also read in reverse. When a previously reported alert disappears after a change, developers and the tools around them often take the vulnerability to be gone. That inference holds only if the analyzer is robust to changes that keep the vulnerability. We test this robustness for CodeQL's JavaScript taint tracking with natural, vulnerability-preserving rewrites. A large language model, given only the alert CodeQL exposes and no knowledge of its implementation, rewrites one function along a reported flow as a plausible maintenance change, and we verify by manual audit and controlled experiments that the flaw survives and the alert does not. On 172 flows that CodeQL detects in real npm vulnerabilities, three rewrites per flow silence 26.2% of them, at about USD 0.51 per silenced flow. The same generator, asked only to refactor the same functions with no knowledge of the alert, silences none of them. Every silencing rewrite traces to one of seven gaps at the library-modeling boundary, and 64 of the 70 rewrites cross a gap inside an API CodeQL already models. The largest is the WHATWG URL constructor, which propagates taint to a URL's query components but not to its pathname. The boundary is not specific to CodeQL. 74% of the silencing rewrites also silence an independently built taint analyzer, and 53% escape three analyzers combined. A disappearing alert after an ordinary-looking change is therefore weak evidence that a vulnerability has been fixed, the gaps point SAST developers to narrow and concrete repair targets, and robustness to natural rewrites belongs alongside detection rate in how taint analyzers are evaluated.
items.title: Preserve the Vulnerability, Break the Alert: Testing the Robustness of CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites

items.summary: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a privilege policy, a dependency graph or a constraint list) that code then enforces. We ask whether small language model (SLM) agents can be trusted to write these artifacts. Across 15 open-weight models, 13 of them between 1.7B and 12B parameters, they cannot: the policies, graphs and constraints that the agent's model writes admit attacks on 14 (Progent), 13 (IPIGuard) and 11 (DRIFT) of the models, and CaMeL's programs fail to run in up to 68% of episodes. We present CapLite, which derives its policy from the tool schemas, commits the write calls before any tool result is read, and admits a write only if every argument that decides whom or what it affects is stated in the user's request. This guarantees write integrity: injected text cannot add a write, and no write reaches a recipient, amount, object or destination that the user did not state. No attack succeeds in 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes. CapLite reaches utility under attack comparable to CaMeL's (29.0% vs. 27.2%) with fewer tokens than every other enforcement defense and than the undefended agent: 17.1k per episode, 18% of CaMeL's, and the highest utility per token of all enforcement defenses.
items.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts

items.summary: An unconditionally secure $(t, s, v)$-all-or-nothing transform (AONT) is a bijection from $s$ input elements to $s$ output elements over an alphabet of size $v$, such that given any $s - t$ output elements, no information can be obtained about any $t$ input elements. While linear AONTs have been extensively studied, comparatively little is known about the existence of non-linear AONTs. In this paper, we investigate unconditionally secure cryptographically non-linear $(t, s, v)$-AONTs, distinguishing between non-additivity, non-affinity, and cryptographic non-linearity. To achieve this, we first present a computational method for enumerating general AONTs focusing on the case $(t, 3, 3)$-AONTs for $t = 1 and 2$, establishing the existence of non-additive AONTs. We then introduce a general construction of non-additive AONTs from linear ones using coordinate-wise symbol permutations. We measure the non-linearity of the AONT instances generated from this construction, using differential $Δ_F$-uniformity and Walsh magnitude. Finally, we establish theoretical conditions under which $Δ_F$-uniformity is reduced and present statistical results examining the non-linearity of AONTs obtained through our construction.
items.title: On cryptographically non-linear all-or-nothing transforms

items.summary: The increasing penetration of inverter-based resources and growing cyber-physical interdependencies expose electrical power systems to disturbances that challenge conventional resilience assessments. Existing approaches often evaluate resilience dimensions independently, overlooking the non-additive effects of coordinated disruptions and the influence of exogenous stressors. To address this gap, this paper proposes a Grid Multidimensional Resilience Index (GRID-MRI) that integrates endogenous disruption severity, coordination effects, and climatic and economic-regulatory conditions. The framework quantifies physical, cyber, and operational degradation, identifies interaction effects through counterfactual (i.e., what-if), simulations of individual and coordinated attacks, and incorporates exogenous stressors as scenario-dependent scaling factors. Its application to a modified IEEE 39-bus system under three escalating cyber-physical attack scenarios, informed by the December 2025 Polish cyberattack incident, reveals that coordinated attacks induce system collapse despite stable individual and additive responses. The corresponding resilience losses are 3.72 and 4.09 times their additive estimates, while GRID-MRI increases from 0.062 to 1.188 and reaches 6.081 under additional exogenous stress. These findings demonstrate the limitations of additive assessments and establish a quantitative basis for distinguishing the dominant mechanisms of multidimensional resilience degradation.
items.title: GRID-MRI: Resilience Assessment of Power Systems under Coordinated Cyber-Physical Attacks

items.summary: Provably secure linguistic steganography assumes that the receiver recovers the sender's tokens, but a text channel delivers only text, and ambiguous tokenizations break extraction. Existing fixes change the distribution, synchronize whole pools of tokens at a capacity that collapses with large vocabularies, or track several token histories. We prove that if extraction is exact and error-free across full-support language models, a single-history receiver is confined to a prefix-free candidate set at every step -- even if it reads the entire future text and the sender constrains later steps -- and must therefore give up the stop entropy, the entropy of deciding whether each prefix token ends there. Fixing these stop decisions on the prefix forest with shared randomness yields coin projection: a closed-form scheme that attains the bound, works with any distribution coder in one model call per token, preserves ordinary sampling, and refines SyncPool for every key. Across English, Chinese and Japanese, ambiguous text is rare (at most 11 in 1,000 tokens), yet the stop entropy at word and morpheme prefixes takes 7.2-9.0% of the entropy at every step; SyncPool's further loss comes from space and single-byte UTF-8 hubs that merge subtrees while carrying almost no stop uncertainty. Coin projection keeps 91-93% of the string entropy for the coder at every vocabulary size; with the full vocabulary, it turns 2.16-6.85 times as much entropy into message bits as SyncPool and recovers every completed message.
items.title: Optimal Single-History Tokenization Disambiguation for Provably Secure Linguistic Steganography

items.summary: FPGAs are widely used in mission-critical systems, where a successful physical attack can have serious consequences. This makes resilience to such attacks a critical security requirement. To defend against active physical attacks, such as glitching attacks, modern FPGAs rely on on-chip sensors that detect these disturbances and trigger responses, such as key zeroization, before a device is compromised. These sensors are deployed as both hard-IP blocks and soft-IP cores, and their trustworthiness is often taken for granted. In this work, we challenge that assumption and argue that the sensors themselves are a fragile and underexplored attack surface. Drawing on recent results, we show that both the detection and response mechanisms of state-of-the-art sensors can be bypassed without invasive tampering. We further argue that sensor reliability is reduced by factors rarely captured in threat models, including the spatial and frequency-dependent behavior of the system's power delivery network, which can steer a fault to a target while sparing nearby sensors; environmental conditions such as temperature, which shift detection thresholds; and long-term aging, which drifts sensor calibration and may open silent detection gaps. Finally, we propose a set of countermeasures that harden detection and response mechanisms against these effects.
items.title: NonSense: On the (In)security of FPGA Anti-tamper Sensors

items.summary: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.
items.title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help

items.summary: Watermark detectors decide whether one document came from a watermarked language model. Auditors often need a different number: the share of a corpus that did. We study this share for Gumbel-max and green-list (KGW) watermarks when every document may have been edited by an unknown amount. Without restrictions on the edits, the upper end of the identified set is 1. Combining a known least-favourable next-token distribution with a sequential coupling, we derive a power envelope indexed by three budgets: a retention floor, an entropy budget, and a budget for in-place substitutions, which for Gumbel-max make edited positions look less watermarked than human text. The envelope gives an identified set that is sharp for the alternatives it dominates, finite-sample bounds on the realized share of a fixed corpus with either the exact null or a null calibrated on an independent human sample, and confidence sequences for streams. In Gumbel-max simulations where the envelope binds, the bounds cover, and the threshold that maximizes the gap between envelope and null is generally as tight as twelve thresholds. On text from OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B, 12,000 fresh human documents scored under three keys show no robust departure from the exact null, and all bounds covered in resampling trials from finite pools of documents with random edits, substitutions and paraphrases; at a share of 0.2 the exact-null bound is about [0.14,0.38]. These results are fragile in two ways we make precise. LLM-paraphrased KGW pools fall below the envelope, yet at 2000 documents the bounds still covered in these trials. A simulated null error of 0.01, comparable to the largest deviation we observed at our thresholds, is likewise harmless at 2000 documents but breaks exact-null coverage at 100,000; a null calibrated on an independent human sample keeps coverage there, but needs a large reference sample to stay narrow.
items.title: Prevalence Bounds for Edited Watermarked Text: Power Envelopes and Calibration Sensitivity

items.summary: In July 2026, the European Commission (EC) set out the anonymization measures Alphabet must implement to share Google Search data with competing search engines under Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act. As the first concrete illustration of how the EC operationalizes anonymization under the EU digital rulebook, this methodology could become a regulatory benchmark. In this paper, we show why it should not. We critically review the anonymization measures proposed by the EC, from the characterization of residual risk to the suppression thresholds and the reliance on contractual safeguards. For each of those issues, we highlight significant conceptual flaws, and, where applicable, we illustrate these flaws with empirical observations from real Google Search data provided by Alphabet and protected under the EC's measures. Importantly, we present examples of low-effort reidentification, record linkage, and confidential attribute inference achieved through straightforward and automatable attack patterns. Our findings show that the approach of the EC relies on unjustified heuristics rather than formal privacy guarantees, underestimates the risks inherent in free-text search queries, and sacrifices data utility without achieving meaningful protection. We also demonstrate that the proposed measures do not meet any of the three anonymization criteria established by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB): no record isolation, no linkage, and no inference. Practitioners and regulators are therefore cautioned against treating these measures as a sound anonymization practice.
items.title: Anonymous in Name Only: A Critical Review and a Reidentification Exercise on the European Commission's Anonymization Measures for Google Search Data under Article 6(11) of the DMA

items.summary: Crypto agility maturity models aim to support organizations in preparing for cryptographic transitions, such as migrating to post-quantum cryptography. Recognizing the importance of measurable maturity, NIST references several such models in its guidance. Given NIST's influence on cybersecurity practice, these models may shape organizational planning and governance mechanisms. However, their design quality has not been systematically evaluated. In this work, we assess three industry-driven maturity models against established design principles. Our analysis reveals recurring weaknesses, particularly the lack of measurable, reproducible assessment criteria and limited prescriptive guidance for improving crypto agility. At the same time, we highlight individual strengths that can assist practitioners in choosing among the models and derive concrete recommendations for strengthening future crypto agility maturity models.
items.title: Maturity$^2$: Assessing the Maturity of Crypto Agility Maturity Models

items.summary: Provably secure linguistic steganography hides a message inside text sampled from a language model, so that without the key, a stegotext is computationally indistinguishable from an honest model sample. Nearly every such scheme assumes the receiver can recompute the sender's token probabilities exactly bit for bit. We show this assumption is fragile: across three model families, bit-exact schemes decode almost none of our messages once the receiver's floating-point precision, quantization, or GPU architecture differs from the sender's, or even when the receiver merely scores a text in parallel versus one token at a time, with the same model, precision, and hardware held fixed. We present STEALTH, a scheme built for exactly this setting. The sender draws each token with an exponential race driven by keyed pseudorandom noise, so a receiver's probability mismatch flips a token only when the race is close; a rateless spinal code, decoded by beam search, absorbs the resulting flips without the sender and receiver ever agreeing on a single distribution. We prove stegotexts remain indistinguishable from honest samples under this construction. Empirically, STEALTH decodes every message we sent for every receiver in the sender's model family, at every precision and quantization level, on smaller models, and on a different GPU architecture. STEALTH is even robust across different model families with separate vocabularies and tokenizers, decoding every message we tested. Our approach carries far more payload per token than prior robust schemes, and trained steganalyzers and a targeted statistical test both fail to distinguish its stegotexts from honest model output.
items.title: STEALTH: Steganographic Text Encoding Agnostic to Low-Level Tensor Hardware

items.summary: An important challenge in homomorphic encryption (HE) is ensuring the integrity of the encrypted computations. Although verifiable computation can address this in theory, making it practical is far from trivial. [Cascudo et al. CRYPTO 2025] recently proposed a solution to this problem for the CKKS scheme. In particular, they propose new succinct arguments that efficiently prove arithmetic circuits and range checks over the ring $R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[Y]/(Y^N+1)$, and combine them to prove computations on CKKS ciphertexts. Despite the important progress, their work faces scalability challenges: the size of the polynomial commitment proofs, a large $O(N)$ overhead in range proofs, and the lack of an explicit method for efficient -- sublinear in circuit size -- verification. In this paper we present new techniques that remove all these bottlenecks. First, we provide a more efficient arithmetization of CKKS computations. Second, we introduce BatchFold, a new polynomial commitment for $R_q$ that supports batched evaluations and achieves shorter proofs. Third, we design packing, a novel algebraic technique that eliminates the need to commit to massive polynomials and removes the $O(N)$ overhead in range proofs. Finally, we introduce SparsePack, an efficient protocol for proving the evaluations of sparse, circuit-dependent polynomials, leveraging both packing and batched evaluations. We evaluate the efficiency of our solution on a generic neural network architecture, achieving proofs several orders of magnitude smaller and faster than prior approaches.
items.title: Batch, Pack, and Prove: More Efficient Verifiable Computation for CKKS

items.summary: Attributing short LLM-generated texts to a specific source remains challenging for existing multi-bit watermarking methods, which often require long generations or costly decoding to recover payloads reliably. We propose a codebook-based watermarking scheme that maps an $n$-bit payload to a longer $u$-bit codeword and embeds it during generation through token-level logit biasing. During extraction, the received bit sequence is matched to the nearest codeword in a precomputed secret codebook using Hamming or Levenshtein distance. Experiments show that our method achieves near-perfect recovery for 16-24 bit payloads on 200-token generations and strong performance on 127-token generations for base models. Results are weaker on some instruction-tuned models with very short texts, where low-entropy output distributions reduce embedding reliability. We also study a BCH-based variant that avoids codebook storage but generally reduces robustness. The Levenshtein variant improves resilience to deletions and light paraphrasing, while insertions and stronger rewrites remain challenging. We analyze collision probability, codeword separation, extraction time, tokenization consistency, and text quality, highlighting both the practicality and limitations of codebook-based watermarking for short-form attribution.
items.title: Look It Up: Multi-bit LLM Watermarking via Codebook Search

items.summary: Private decision-tree evaluation lets a server classify a client's encrypted query without learning the input. In the non-interactive, path-based setting over TFHE, the server returns a single encrypted prediction by aggregating per-path comparison outcomes, and the standard per-leaf formulation pays one programmable bootstrap (PBS) per leaf, which dominates the cost. We propose a signed dyadic path-sum encoding that nearly halves this cost: each internal node receives a signed dyadic label so that every root-to-leaf path accumulates a distinct integer sum, which lets the two children of a leaf-parent be packed into a single test polynomial and resolved by one PBS, reducing the PBS count from the number of leaves to the number of leaf-parents. We formalize the distinct-sum property and prove that the dyadic labeling is the range-minimal encoding satisfying it, and its half-symmetric signed form is magnitude-optimal, tightening the comparison-stage noise bound at fixed parameters. We derive the two conditions under which the encrypted evaluation returns the exact prediction and instantiate parameters with per-inference failure below $2^{-64}$ at 128-bit security. We show that the ring degree grows linearly with the consumed plaintext range, which confines the profitable regime to depths $\leq 4$, where our method stays faster even when each scheme runs at its own cost-optimal parameters. We further extend the encoding to gradient-boosted ensembles. On standard UCI benchmarks at depths 1-4, our method reduces single-tree latency by $1.51\times$-$1.92\times$ and ensemble latency by $2\times$, without accuracy loss, while preserving the compact, non-interactive response.
items.title: Signed Dyadic Path Encoding for Efficient Non-Interactive Private Decision Tree Evaluation over TFHE

items.summary: Mobile GUI agents read the screen of a phone and operate apps on a user's behalf to complete multi-step tasks such as online shopping or messaging. Because the agent acts on whatever the screen shows, an attacker can embed malicious instructions into ordinary UI content and redirect its actions. We refer to this threat as environmental injection attack (EIA). Existing benchmarks measure this risk by pinning hand-crafted payloads to a fixed step of a fixed task. This approach faces two limitations. First, each payload is bound to one task in one app and does not transfer without manual redesign. Second, agents given the same task may follow different routes, so an agent that never reaches the injected page is recorded as safe without being tested. This insufficient test coverage can cause fixed-point benchmarks to underestimate the security risk of deployed mobile agents. In this work, we propose MobileProbe, a trajectory-aware red-teaming framework that evaluates mobile agents adaptively. MobileProbe discovers attacker-controllable content surfaces through automated pentesting, localizes vulnerable decision points along the agent's trajectory, and iteratively refines context-aware payloads through a surrogate-filtered evolutionary loop. We construct a benchmark of 83 long-horizon attack instances spanning 12 mobile applications. Each is annotated with a Confidentiality, Integrity, or Availability (CIA) attack goal to cover the principal categories of security threats facing mobile agents. On three representative agent architectures, MobileProbe attains higher attack success rates than human-written, zero-shot LLM, and prior automated red-teaming baselines adapted to the mobile domain. MobileProbe can serve as a pre-deployment auditing tool to systematically uncover vulnerabilities and inform security hardening of mobile agents.
items.title: MobileProbe: Adaptive Security Evaluation of Mobile Agents via Trajectory-Aware Injection

items.summary: Affected-version ranges in vulnerability databases decide which deployments scanners, patching pipelines, and incident responders treat as vulnerable, yet these ranges are often incomplete, so vulnerable releases are silently treated as safe. Auditing them requires executable evidence: given a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for a listed version, show that the same vulnerability can be triggered on an earlier, unlisted version. This cross-version PoC migration combines source-code analysis, environment repair, and execution-based verification. We introduce CrossPloit, a benchmark of 127 migration instances across 45 CVEs in the Python web ecosystem. Each instance includes a version-pinned container, a reference PoC, and a vulnerability-specific oracle; two validators check that the observed effect arises from the disclosed vulnerability. Benchmark construction confirms 149 vulnerable prior versions absent from the affected-version lists of four databases, 127 of which require migration. Across 18 agent configurations (nine models and two harnesses), the best configuration resolves 58.3% of instances, compared with 8.7% for an adapted trace-guided baseline. Attack-vector shifts are particularly difficult: no configuration resolves more than 37.9% of these instances. Higher resolve rates are associated with a smaller share of missed-API failures and a larger share of incomplete executions among the remaining failures. In one configuration, withholding the reference PoC and its environment specification reduces resolve rate from 50.4% to 15.0%, highlighting the value of the supplied reference package. CrossPloit provides an execution-based measurement of under-reported exposure and of how far its enumeration can be automated.
items.title: CrossPloit: A Benchmark for Cross-Version PoC Migration in Python Web Applications

items.summary: We ask whether small, open-weight decision models can support vulnerability discovery in open-source software at scale and what the surrounding system must provide. These models answer a typed question in one forward pass, returning scores for the permitted answers rather than text. Our harness selects widely packaged C and C++ projects and uses deterministic incomplete-fix miners and shape localizers to decide where to look. Intern-Decision-4B, a 4B-parameter open-weight decision model, then scores every candidate function. The scores rank the queues rather than accept or reject candidates, apart from a low reach-score floor that some queues kept. The search uses no frontier model. Alone, the model is weak: it separates vulnerable from benign functions with AUC 0.73, but a vulnerable function from its own patch with only 0.56. It is more useful for ordering candidates. On 75 public CVEs from projects without any of our findings, the fixed function reached its repository's top 25 in 21% of cases, 1.4 times as often as under random order of the same queues. Recall is bounded mainly by where the localizers look. On the campaign's own queues the model's order placed 7.5 times more confirmed findings in the top 10 than random order, an observed, selection-biased upper bound. On three GB10 systems, the harness searched more than 4,000 projects at 900-1,100 repositories per hour. The campaign confirmed 187 memory-safety findings; by worst-case CVSS v3.1, 12 are critical, 148 high, 23 medium and 4 low. The decision step runs at 4.4 decisions per second on one GB10 and 9.8 on a consumer RTX 4090 gaming PC, with matching scores. A small decision model supports vulnerability discovery through prioritization, while deterministic analysis and verification remain essential. All confirmed findings are being disclosed to maintainers under coordinated disclosure before publication.
items.title: Look Here, Then Decide: Small Decision Models in a Harness Find Memory-Safety Vulnerabilities at Scale on Commodity GPUs

items.summary: We consider a physical layer authentication scenario in which a legitimate user (Alice) communicates with an authen- ticator (Bob) through a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS), controlled by Bob. An attacker (Trudy) aims to impersonate Alice by suitably precoding her messages and still transmitting them through the RIS. This two-part study analyzes this attack-defense interaction between Bob and Trudy under perfect (Part I) and partial (Part II) channel knowledge by all the agents. Part I formulates the joint RIS selection and precoder design under perfect channel knowledge as a finite zero-sum game, establishing exact channel subspace conditions for attack indistinguishability alongside equilibrium mixed strategies. Part II extends the defense to incomplete channel information, where each agent observes only its own channel, by formulating a finite-action Bayesian game and characterizing the resulting Bayesian Nash equilibrium. Simulations in geometric and 3GPP TR 38.901 UMi-NLOS channels reveal that authentication performance is governed by available spatial degrees of freedom, channel correlation, and operating signal-to-noise ratio. The proposed equilibrium strategies effectively balance communication rate and security, outperforming conventional benchmark policies.
items.title: Game-Theoretic Analysis of RIS-Assisted Challenge-Response PLA - Part I: Perfect Channel Knowledge

items.summary: Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search has become a fundamental query primitive in modern vector databases for managing large-scale embedding data. To support growing vector collections, organizations increasingly outsource database management and query processing to third-party clouds. However, untrusted service providers may return suboptimal or fabricated results, posing a serious threat to ANN search integrity. Existing authenticated ANN approaches face substantial scalability challenges. They typically require transmitting high-dimensional vectors for distance verification and rely on topology-agnostic authentication structures, resulting in excessive communication and verification overhead. In this paper, we propose VIDA, a novel and efficient scheme for authenticated graph-based ANN search. VIDA replaces raw vector transmission with compact vector commitments and employs an aggregated Inner Product Argument to efficiently verify multiple distance computations. Furthermore, we introduce MeST, a topology-aware authenticated data structure that aligns authentication paths with graph traversal, significantly reducing structural proof overhead. Additionally, we design a quantization-aware authentication strategy that exploits distance bounds for pruning, reducing the number of exact distances requiring cryptographic authentication. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed schemes substantially improve the efficiency of authenticated ANN search, achieving up to a $6.6\times$ speedup in end-to-end latency and reducing data transfer time by up to 99.2% compared with state-of-the-art methods.
items.title: Authenticated Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in Outsourced Vector Databases

items.summary: The game "Mafia'' is a social deduction game where $n$ players attempt to uncover a covert coalition of $m$ players among the $n$. Typically, $d=1$ of the non-coalition players are labelled ``Detective'' and have special abilities. Most game-theoretic analysis considers, however, only the variant without a Detective. Once the Detective role is introduced, extremely complex strategies can be employed, for which reason only upper and lower bounds for winning have been established, namely by considering specific strategies. We analyse the case $m=d=1$, providing a first example where an explicit, provably-optimal strategy can be described beyond $d=0$.
items.title: How to Defeat a Mafia (of Size 1)

items.summary: We implement privacy-preserving local electricity exchanges using an automated market maker on the Hyperledger Besu network under QBFT consensus. The proposed protocol operator collects individual electricity positions off-chain and publishes aggregate supply and demand on the blockchain, where smart contracts compute market prices every fifteen minutes. Individual positions remain off-chain; Poseidon2 commitments and UltraHonk zeroknowledge proofs, generated from Noir circuits, verify aggregation, payments, and daily balance updates. The architecture retains community coordination while making financial execution independently auditable. Signed receipts and member-triggered recourse prevent unverified or partial settlement. In a ten-household experiment using simulated US residential profiles, daily settlement uses approximately 19 million gas and produces eight-member proofs in 2.4 seconds. Over four simulated days, local trading covers 34.4% of demand and reduces grid-only costs by 30.5% under assumed tariffs. Numerically computed __-Nash Equilibrium electricity profiles capture 83-88% of the social planner surplus.
items.title: Verifiable Settlement and Pricing for Local Energy Markets: Architecture and Deployment on Hyperledger Besu

items.summary: We expose a safety vulnerability on nascent agentic reinforcement-learning-as-a-service. Specifically, with a cost as low as \$20, we show that safety alignment of a large language model (e.g., Inkling) can be completely subverted through rounds of harmful agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL) with a toxic environment from its users. We also demonstrate that upon a successful harmful agentic RL attack via the service API, the attackers can potentially use the safety-degraded model to assist with real-world harmful activities, e.g., exploit software vulnerabilities and launch code re-use attacks. To mitigate harmful agentic RL, we propose Bait, a defense that mitigates the attack via proactively probing the reward function. Experimental results show that such a simple defense can sufficiently mitigate learning from a harmful reward function and can still learn from a benign reward function that promotes benign agentic tasks. Further analysis on both empirical and theoretical aspects shows that an adaptive attacker who assumes the knowledge of Bait defense cannot perfectly subvert it due to a systematic challenge. Source code is available at https://github.com/git-disl/Bait.
items.title: Bait: Mitigating Harmful Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Probing Reward Function

items.summary: Generative image editing facilitates content creation but complicates source attribution and edit verification. Existing watermarking methods combine copyright protection with tamper localization, yet background reconstruction can weaken spatial evidence even when source identifiers remain recoverable. We propose ReliaGuard, a reconstruction-aware watermarking framework for source attribution and blind edit localization. The writer optimizes keyed feature responses in both the protected image and its variational autoencoder reconstruction under image-distortion and source-preservation constraints. Using only the received image and a secret key, the reader combines watermark responses with local image context through residual evidence refinement and predicts an edit mask through native-resolution-guided multiscale reading. It is trained on complete editing outputs, locally spliced counterparts, and processed versions of both. On an independent test set of 300 source images and 900 editing cases from three image domains, our method achieves edit-region intersection-over-union scores of 85.61% for complete outputs and 94.90% for locally spliced outputs at a threshold calibrated to a nominal 1% background false-positive rate on complete outputs. The complete-output result exceeds the strongest baseline by 45.02 percentage points, while decoded identifier-bit accuracy reaches 100% in both conditions. Across seven families of image processing, the corresponding localization scores are 81.01% and 86.49%, with identifier-bit accuracies of 92.76% and 92.79%, respectively. These results support source recovery and blind edit localization under background reconstruction and subsequent image processing.
items.title: ReliaGuard: Reconstruction-Aware Watermarking for Source Attribution and Blind Edit Localization

items.summary: Bitcoin's Lightning payment network returns the funds of a channel that cannot close cooperatively through pre-signed transactions whose fees and delays fall on its operators. That fee design is being replaced: Bitcoin Core 31.0 removed the mempool rule anchor channels relied on, and the Lightning specification adopted zero-fee commitments in May 2026. What the old design costs has never been measured across fee regimes. We trace every public channel close and every force close on-chain from January 2018 to October 2026, 973,581 closes, and follow each output to its spend. A separate chain index confirms all 698,476 public closes we could compare. Fee spikes did not bring a wave of force closes. Force closes in a spike week and the next were 0.97 times the four weeks before, against 1.02 after ordinary weeks of the same years. A force close costs 2-6 times a cooperative close in fees and locks the closer's balance for days, which outweighs the fees only in low-fee years. When fees are high, pending payments are exposed: in 2023, 18.2% of HTLC timeouts confirmed more than 40 blocks after expiry. Yet since 2021, forwarding nodes lost only 38 payments, each with the preimage already on-chain. Anchor outputs cut late timeouts in fee spikes (20.6% against 30.5%), yet owners rarely bump commitments with them, and miners take most of what third parties sweep. Zero-fee commitments would save only 12% of the anchor mechanism's block space; they should be judged by how promptly payments resolve when fees spike.
items.title: What Does It Cost to Force-Close a Lightning Channel? Evidence from 974,000 Channel Closes, 2018-2026

items.summary: We introduce SEC, an expander-code-based ramp secret sharing scheme over $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, particularly suitable for lattice-based distributed cryptography. It is everywhere-short: bounded secret coefficients yield bounded share coefficients, and the integer reconstruction vectors have bounded entries. Moreover, each participant receives exactly one share, regardless of the number of parties and the privacy and reconstruction thresholds. This improves on prior schemes with bounded share coefficients and bounded entries in the integer reconstruction vectors, in which the number of sub-shares or shares per participant grows either with the number of parties and the threshold or with the security parameter. The construction rests on a coding-theoretic observation: in the bi-adjacency matrix of a lossless bipartite expander, unique-neighbor peeling completes every sufficiently small set of columns to a square unimodular submatrix. We prove correctness, everywhere-shortness, and linearity, and give a publicly computable entrywise bound on the reconstruction vector our algorithm returns for each authorized set. For privacy, we introduce hard-core local leakage resilience, which strengthens the leakage-resilience notion of Nielsen and Simkin (EUROCRYPT 2020) to protect a hard-core function of the secret, and we prove that SEC satisfies it against correlated multi-query local leakage under the MatrixHint-MLWE problem, which admits a reduction from the standard MLWE problem. For $n=60$ participants and security parameter $κ=128$, SEC achieves privacy threshold 6 against $2^{64}$ leakage queries and empirical reconstruction threshold 46. The ideal entropy-coded secret and share sizes are about 3.5 KiB and 6.4 KiB, respectively.
items.title: SEC: One-Share Everywhere-Short Secret Sharing from Lossless Expanders

items.summary: Firewall log classification is important to monitor network traffic. Machine learning classifiers using network-related features have shown good results for this task, but high-dimensional features slow down classification. In this paper, we apply feature selection using bee swarm optimization with Q-learning-based local search (QBSO-FS) to the UCI Internet Firewall Data Set, together with random forest (RF), k-nearest neighbor (KNN), and Bernoulli naïve Bayes (Bernoulli NB) classifiers. The first version of this preprint selected and evaluated feature subsets on the same 5-fold cross-validation of the full data set, which contains 12.8\% exact duplicates; the reported scores are therefore optimistically biased. In this extended version, we re-evaluate the method with a leakage-free protocol: the data are split into training, validation, and test sets, features are selected using the validation set only, and accuracy and macro-averaged scores are measured once on the untouched test set, for both the raw data and a deduplicated, preprocessed version. On a single stratified split, QBSO-FS selects 5--7 features. The selected subsets clearly improve Macro-F1 over all features for KNN on both data sets and for RF on the deduplicated data (by 8--19 percentage points). For RF on the raw data and for Bernoulli NB, the differences (0.2--1.5 percentage points) may not hold for a different split. RF with 7 selected features reaches 99.90\% accuracy and 94.88\% Macro-F1 on the deduplicated data. On the same split, this exceeds our re-implementations of the deep neural network configurations of previous studies and the feature subset selected by particle swarm optimization in one of them, while the run time saved on this low-dimensional data set is small. These results suggest that the method can support automatic firewall log analysis, while evaluation over multiple splits remains future work.
items.title: Optimal feature selection for firewall log analysis using Machine learning and Hybrid Metaheuristic algorithms

items.summary: LLM agents apply approval settings, such as whether to ask before a consequential tool call, through instructions in their system prompt, and operators keep these settings confidential by restricting access to prompts and responses. Audits check whether an agent obeys its setting, not whether a neighboring process can infer which setting is deployed. PolicySniff infers an agent's approval-policy state through shared-GPU execution. A co-resident attacker that knows the candidate settings and the task first profiles both settings, then times only its own GPU kernels while the agent processes the task. The policy prefix is cached before capture, so the attacker observes processing of a task suffix that is identical under both settings. On an eager sparse mixture-of-experts runtime, where each selected expert runs as separate work, a frozen and blinded study identified the deployed setting at 94.17% balanced accuracy on its primary estimand. Across all authorization conditions, accuracy was 88.82% on tasks for which both settings produce the same decision and 91.98% on tasks where they differ. Hardware replays of expert routing show that its temporal density and layer-and-bucket alignment carry the policy information. Behavioral compliance does not imply configuration confidentiality: deployments that keep their approval setting private should measure its distinguishability on the serving runtime and enforce authorization outside the model.
items.title: PolicySniff: Inferring Agent Policy States through Shared-GPU Execution

items.summary: Hardware fault injection attacks threaten machine learning systems, yet their impact on reinforcement learning (RL) has received little attention despite the use of RL in safety-critical applications. This paper presents a security analysis of Q-Learning implementations under voltage and clock glitching attacks on a ChipWhisperer platform, evaluating five variants: Standard, Robust, Resilient, Linear, and Deep Q-Learning. In standard Q-Table implementations, faults corrupt reward computation, action selection, and Q-value updates during learning, and change the selected action during inference. Robust Q-Learning does not prevent these attacks: NaN and infinite values injected during learning persist in the Q-table, and its greedy policy uses the same code as standard Q-Learning. This paper also evaluates a Resilient Q-Learning variant that applies triple modular redundancy with majority voting. It corrects corruption of a single Q-table copy, but inputs shared by the copies, such as the reward, and the voting code itself remain outside its protection. The analysis extends to Linear and Deep Q-Learning, where faults corrupt stored weights during learning and change actions during inference. Moving beyond benchmark environments, this work evaluates an online traffic light controller in a microscopic traffic simulator, where a single injected infinite value degrades accumulated vehicle waiting time by 148x while corrupting under 4% of the Q-table, and where triple modular redundancy corrected the faults injected in our tests, although glitching could still halt the device. Altogether, this work provides a basis for understanding and securing RL deployments against fault injection attacks.
items.title: Fault Injection Attacks on Q-Learning: Analysis, Vulnerabilities, and Countermeasures

items.summary: The CoordX Protocol carries signed and encrypted entries between parties. It proves who wrote each entry and who had permission to write it. It does not say what an entry means. That task belongs above the protocol layer. This paper describes the CoordX type system, the layer that gives entries a meaning. A type is a short document that says how to read one part of a shared record: which entries count, what each position means, what a party may do there, and what a party must do next. The type system has two key properties. It is trustless: a type is an ordinary signed object fixed by its digest, and every party evaluates it for itself over entries that the CoordX Protocol has already verified. No party has to trust a server, a registry or another party's software. It is swappable: a type names the interpreter it is written for, so many interpreters, of different capabilities and designs, can be used side by side in one record. We describe how to write type schemas, and we define the expressive power of the schema language. Payloads form a regular language. Entry structure forms a regular tree language. Every rule and every computed value is a total function in the primitive recursive class, so evaluation always halts. We compare this with KQML, FIPA-ACL and CBCL, and we relate it to language-theoretic security.
items.title: CoordX Types: A Trustless, Swappable Type System for Shared Records

items.summary: AI agents increasingly access enterprise data, invoke powerful tools, and act with limited human oversight. Existing security defenses primarily detect prompt injection, harmful outputs, or suspicious behavior, but do not determine whether an agent remains faithful to the purpose for which it was deployed. An action may contain no attack pattern and stay within granted permissions while still violating the agent's role, organizational constraints, or purpose. We introduce Intent- Aware Security, a framework that treats trusted agent intent as a first-class security object. We define Intent Preservation and Intent Drift, and operationalize them through an Intent Profile: an agent-specific representation extracted from organizational, role, and developer intent. We further introduce an Intent-Aware benchmark of 887 validated samples across 35 agents, built by a generation procedure that fixes ground-truth labels before LLM realization, and four Intent Profile-based protections: pre-execution detection, post-execution detection, input alignment, and system-prompt hardening. Across all evaluations, Intent Profile-based protection outperforms all profile-free baselines on the primary metric. On our benchmark, it raises four-class acro-F1 from 45% to 79% (Out-of-Scope F1 from 8% to 76%). On more than 10,000 executed AgentDojo trajectories, where ground truth comes from environment state, profile-based post-execution detection reaches 0.949 AUROC versus AlignmentCheck 0.909, 0.897 with raw agent configuration and 0.843 without context. Profile-based input alignment improves protection success by 7 points over DataFilter with a comparable benign utility. These results suggest that an agent's intended purpose can serve as a useful security reference for detecting and mitigating deviations from its deployed role and operational boundaries.
items.title: Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents

items.summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a cornerstone of 6G networks, enabling simultaneous data transmission and environmental perception. However, the ubiquitous radiation of sensing waveforms introduces a critical security vulnerability where the physical existence and characteristics of targets are continuously exposed to unauthorized wardens. Meanwhile, existing sensing-secure methods primarily focus on degrading a target warden's parameter-estimation accuracy, yet they fail to prevent wardens from detecting the target's physical presence. In this article, we first analyze sensing security threats in ISAC systems and survey existing sensing-secure methods. To address the critical gap, we propose a novel security paradigm termed endogenous target covertness. By intentionally harnessing environmental scatterers, such as known objects, ambient backscatter devices, and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), as ghost targets, the proposed scheme ensures a low probability that the warden detects the true target for the true target at the warden. This deliberately renders the true target's existence indistinguishable to the warden, while the legitimate base station can extract the true target's response using prior knowledge of the scatterers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme through a case study, proving that absolute target covertness can be achieved without consuming dedicated jamming power. Finally, we outline key open challenges and promising research directions to realize truly secure, ubiquitous sensing in future ISAC ecosystems.
items.title: Harnessing Environmental Scatterers for Endogenous Target Covertness in 6G ISAC: A New Paradigm for Sensing Security

items.summary: In this paper, we introduce low probability of target detection (LPTD) as a new security objective for wireless sensing systems, where the existence of a target is concealed from passive wardens. Unlike conventional communication security and covert communication, LPTD aims to protect the sensed target itself from malicious detection, rather than concealing transmitted signals or communication activities. Specifically, we propose a reconfigurable-antenna-based reflector-assisted target covertness scheme, where passive reflectors deployed around the target are harnessed as artificial scattering sources to confuse the warden. By adjusting their reflection coefficients, these reflectors reshape the local scattering environment and mask the target-induced echo. We then analyze the warden's optimal detection strategy and derive the false-alarm and missed-detection probabilities, followed by a closed-form expression for its minimum total detection error probability. Numerical results validate the analysis and show that sufficient cooperation among reflectors can increase the warden's minimum total detection error probability to approximately 0.94--0.96, making target detection close to random guessing.
items.title: Low Probability of Target Detection in Wireless Sensing by Harnessing Reconfigurable-antenna based Reflectors

items.summary: We study the average one-guess success probability of an adversary who observes the ordinary integer sum of a finite-support secret and an independent integer-valued mask, subject to an absolute-moment budget on the mask. For a uniform secret on an interval the exact optimum and an explicit optimiser are obtained. For a biased bit the masks that achieve no increase over the prior baseline are characterised and their minimal cost is determined. The entire cost-vulnerability frontier is then determined for every bias. It is the piecewise-linear interpolation of an explicit sequence of points generated by cost-optimally shifted truncated geometric masks. It has infinitely many affine pieces, which accumulate at the critical cost, where the frontier meets the prior baseline with zero slope. The proof rests on a layer-cake decomposition of an arbitrary mask into truncated geometrics, along which both the vulnerability and the cost are exactly additive. The results give exact design guidance for additive integer noise under the average one-guess metric; they do not constitute a cryptographic masking scheme.
items.title: Optimal Additive Integer Masks for One-Guess Vulnerability under an Absolute-Moment Budget

items.summary: Federated learning (FL) systems increasingly rely on blockchain based reward mechanisms to incentivize participation while preserving data privacy. We design and empirically evaluate two complementary Solidity smart contracts for FL reward distribution: the first one that allocates rewards proportionally to a publicly disclosed quality score, and a privacy preserving variant that hides individual quality scores behind a zero-knowledge (ZK) proof of a threshold condition. Both contracts mint a non transferable, use-and-burn token maintaining a trustless incentive structure. We evaluate the two designs through MNIST training with adversarial behavior, including Sybil attacks, zero gradient and random noise, across three independent random seeds. Our results reveal a fundamental tradeoff between cryptographic privacy and incentive fairness. The privacy preserving architecture strictly degrades system robustness, doubling the adversary's average reward capture while introducing severe outcome variance. This vulnerability is driven by a structural self-inclusion bias within cosine-similarity scoring: as the global model converges, legitimate gradient updates naturally diminish, rendering them statistically indistinguishable from bounded noise. Adversaries exploit this dynamic to systematically breach the ZK threshold, triggering a late stage failure cascade that culminates in absolute adversary monopoly over the reward pool and the total exclusion of honest contributors. Alongside a closed-form theorem formalizing this privacy--Sybil resistance tradeoff, we map strict mainnet deployment boundaries via linear gas scaling models, explicitly incorporating the post-Fusaka EIP-7825 per transaction gas cap. Ultimately, while cryptographically secure, static threshold ZK gates fail as incentive layer fairness mechanisms under realistic FL convergence dynamics on standard benchmarks.
items.title: Tokenized Reward Systems for Federated Learning: The Privacy vs. Fairness Tradeoff

items.summary: Personalized LLM services place private facts and application instructions into a prompt, then retain representations of that context for later inference. Latent-state LLMs compress part of this history into fixed-size recurrent state. The information preserved by its learned updates is implicit, and later computation can expose it even when an observer receives neither the private text nor the responses. We investigate privacy leakage from recurrent state through partial-state probing and physical observation of its use. Our methodology separates recoverable information, persistence through public dialogue, causal influence on later decisions, and leakage through power. Experiments with released hybrid implementations show that a small state observation supports multiple predictions about private facts and response rules, and that personal attributes generalize to unseen authors. The information remains inferable after public dialogue and changes later decision margins. Complete-read power recovers private facts under a fixed execution schedule. On a partitioned GPU, an unprivileged account infers age from whole-device power during public requests; a separate state-isolation experiment establishes the recurrent contribution to this channel. These findings extend context confidentiality to the lifetime and execution of retained state. They identify access-control responsibilities for serving systems, telemetry restrictions for GPU operators, and data-dependent power leakage for accelerator designers.
items.title: Privacy Leakage from Recurrent State in LLM Inference

items.summary: Feature-attribution methods can query rule-violating network states through perturbations, coalitions, references, paths, and ablations, making explanations and their evaluation sensitive to model behavior outside the operational domain. We formalize this failure mode as domain blindness and prove valid-query invariance: when models agree on the required oracle information within a declared rule-valid set, a procedure confined to that set returns the same attribution. We instantiate one protocol-aware query-control principle in LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, and DeepLIFT and audit paired configurations across four NIDS datasets and three classifier families. In six settings where standard LIME reports perfect top-feature repeatability, PA-LIME reveals substantial variability, with a mean of 0.575. Under FGSM followed by protocol repair, PA-DeepLIFT and PA-IG achieve the largest attribution-similarity curve areas, 0.452 and 0.413, while mean within-PA rank agreement rises to 0.366 from 0.217. PA-XAI therefore turns structured domain assumptions into explicit, testable controls for explanation auditing; support modeling, raw-flow reconstruction, and adaptive explanation attacks provide complementary validation layers.
items.title: Protocol-Aware Auditing of Domain-Blind Feature Attribution in Network Intrusion Detection

items.summary: Static Random Access Memory (SRAM) Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) are a promising technology in the realm of random number generation for key generation, but for PUF-based authentication, they have been sidelined due to their limited challenge space as a reservoir of Challenge-Response Pairs (CRPs). In this paper, we develop a seed-based, round-iterated feedback mechanism, which we name Device-Unique Feedback Traversal (DUFT). The feedback chain is driven by the device's unstable and stable bit positions in its stability mask against the address to create a unique traversal. Additionally, a device-key hashed from the unique SRAM-PUF array is also included in calculating the next round of the chain to keep it secret. By estimating the physical SRAM source's entropy and error rate empirically, or by having a source with established metrics in both, DUFT estimates the number of rounds of feedback in the traversal to be performed to achieve a certain amount of min-entropy. We reach 128 bits of estimated min-entropy on our reference hardware under stated assumptions and experimental estimates. The number of rounds in the traversal scales directly with measured source-entropy, allowing security to be increased for weaker sources at the cost of running time. Using this feedback-traversal wrapper over SRAM-PUFs to obtain a measured-response, we propose an extremely lightweight authentication and key-encapsulation protocol for resource-constrained embedded devices. We realize and evaluate DUFT end-to-end on physical IoT/embedded hardware: a discrete-SRAM node pair running the complete mechanism and end-to-end protocol, and an embedded-SRAM microcontroller for the mechanism alone.
items.title: DUFT: Device-Unique Feedback Traversal for Entropy-Estimated Response Extraction and Mutual Authentication using SRAM PUFs

items.summary: Tendermint is a consensus protocol that tolerates Byzantine faults, implemented first by the Tendermint Core engine and now by CometBFT. Realizing the protocol's separation of agreement from execution, the Application Blockchain Interface (ABCI) of these engines keeps consensus apart from the replicated application, so one engine can serve many independent proof-of-stake chains. A sustained body of research proposes changes that span the protocol's mechanisms, from vote dissemination to block proposal and reward distribution, yet to our knowledge no survey studies the protocol and these works as one family, and broader surveys do not take Tendermint as their subject. We describe the baseline, the protocol as consolidated from its original descriptions, by its design choices. Each is a decision, such as how votes spread or how proposers rotate, through which the baseline provides safety and liveness or another property under its fault and timing model. We classify each work by the design choice it renegotiates, that is, modifies or replaces, by the properties it strengthens or weakens, and by whether its result needs a stronger model. Taking a broader perspective on that classification, we group the surveyed works' solutions into a few threads of concern in the baseline, namely its performance, the accountability of its validators, and the protection of exploitable information. For each thread, we identify the recurring strategies that their approaches follow. Together, these threads and strategies describe the current state of research on the Tendermint family. Where the strategies leave gaps, we pose future directions, each as an open question under an explicit fault and timing model.
items.title: SoK: Design Choices in Tendermint BFT Consensus

items.summary: In spectrum coexistence systems, the primary user (PU) activity must be partially disclosed for interference avoidance and coordination, while the exact spectrum occupancy information is often restricted due to security and regulatory constraints. To this end, subset-based disclosures can be employed in which the true frequency is included while ambiguity is introduced. This paper shows that naive randomized subset disclosures remain highly vulnerable to information leakage through inference, as temporal structure can be exploited to recover spectrum usage information. Under Markovian dynamics of the PU's spectrum usage, hidden Markov model (HMM) filtering with online learning is applied, while under periodic dynamics, period and phase estimations with phase-aligned statistics are used for inference. To address this vulnerability, structure-aware obfuscation strategies are introduced. For Markovian dynamics, history-based and belief-based schemes are designed to induce model mismatch and limit posterior concentration, while for periodic dynamics, cycle-dominance and decoy-based schemes are designed to manipulate phase-wise statistics and bias the inference process. These obfuscation schemes significantly hinder inference of spectrum information and offer principled disclosure solutions for spectrum coexistence systems.
items.title: Privacy-Preserving Spectrum Data Obfuscation in Next-Generation Spectrum Coexistence Systems

items.summary: A vulnerability detector is only as trustworthy as the benchmark that scores it, and today's real-world datasets tend to flatter detectors. They are often built once and never refreshed, so they quickly miss new vulnerabilities, their labels are either noisy or heavily filtered, and their random splits let models train on near-copies of test code and on future vulnerabilities. Above all, when a fix only adds code, such as a missing NULL check, they do not point at where the vulnerability was, preventing detectors from learning to localize some of the most common C/C++ weaknesses. We present VulSpot, a living benchmark for detecting, classifying, and localizing vulnerabilities, with over 500k functions in 21 languages from 24k registered CVEs, including over 15k vulnerable C/C++ functions. By linking the code added by a patch to the existing statement it protects, VulSpot locates the vulnerability in 99.3\% of the functions that previous diff-based datasets used to leave without a location. Rather than discarding uncertain labels, it tells users how reliable each one is, and it comes with leak-free splits, complementary code context, and hierarchical CWE labels. An automated pipeline refreshes VulSpot every month, so that each release brings vulnerabilities no model has seen yet.
items.title: Beyond the Diff - VulSpot: A Vulnerability Dataset Where No Vulnerability Goes Unlocalized

items.summary: In this work, we ask whether an attacker can go beyond detecting a hidden image and tell what it depicts, even without knowing which model hid it. We show that, for deep image hiding, this is surprisingly easy. To test this, we build an evaluation dataset of stego images generated by 11 hiding models. These models span two families (invertible neural networks and autoencoders), use different backbones (CNN, Transformer, and Mamba), and include both spatial- and frequency-domain hiding methods. We demonstrate that training HiNet [17] in the usual way yields a single decoder that can extract secret content from unseen models across these settings. Both humans and machines can recognize what it reveals. A frequency analysis shows that most models favor mid- and high-frequency embedding. Guided by this finding, we strengthen cross-model extraction by enhancing cover textures and suppressing secret textures during training. The attack extends to out-of-distribution secrets and to multi-image hiding. It even exposes private content hidden by AIRPNet [13], a recent image restoration method that uses steganography for privacy protection. What surprised us most is that decoders from every hiding model we test exhibit this ''universal'' extraction ability to varying degrees. Our code and datasets will be open-sourced.
items.title: Your Secrets Are Showing: Deep Image Hiding Models Are Surprisingly Easy to Attack

items.summary: Synthetic data is increasingly important in data usage and AI design, creating novel legal and policy dilemmas. All too often, discussions of synthetic data treat it as entirely distinct from "real," collected data, overlooking the risks posed by different kinds and uses of synthetic data. We build on Michal Gal and Orla Lynskey's argument that synthetic data will transform information privacy, market competition, and data quality. While the risks posed by synthetic data depend on its connection to collected data, we argue that background knowledge and assumptions about ground truth used to create it are at least as important. We bring that focus to Gal and Lynskey's taxonomy of synthetic data, arguing that this focus is essential to grasp synthetic data's legal and policy implications. As such, we divide synthetic data into (1) transformed data, which modifies collected data to preserve certain statistical properties for an end use; (2) augmented data, which relies on assumptions to bolster a collected dataset's fidelity to the ground truth; and (3) simulated data, which relies almost entirely on background knowledge and ground-truth assumptions. Applying this taxonomy, we show that no category of synthetic data prevents privacy harms from group-based inferences, that augmented and simulated data can amplify bias while making a dataset look more complete, and that synthetic data rarely lets smaller competitors overcome incumbents' data advantages. As policymakers weigh whether to incentivize, mandate, or discourage the use of synthetic data, they should consider the validity of the ground-truth assumptions used in producing that data.
items.title: Taxonomizing Synthetic Data for Law

items.summary: Signed PDF documents have legally binding value under frameworks such as the EU's eIDAS regulation. In this work, we present Genuine PDF Forgeries, a novel attack class that focuses on human factors in signature validation. Our attacks target the disconnect between cryptographically verifiable signer certificates and human-visible signature blocks embedded in documents. We analyze our attacks against 23 PDF viewers and validation tools across desktop platforms and the web. We find that nine of the 13 viewers that automatically report signature validity hide authenticated signer information behind additional user interaction. We then evaluate the attack in twin deception-based online studies with 584 EU-based participants. To further validate the impact, we perform a highly tailored real-world attack study with six trials within two privacy-sensitive organizations. Five of six organizational trials accepted requests authenticated using the forged visual identity. In the online studies (total n=584), the most effective attack variant deceives 71.9% of eligible participants on first impression, and 57.3% continue to be deceived even after we prompt for additional introspection. We derive viewer-side countermeasures and prototype a safeguard that overlays the untrusted signature block with signer information obtained from the validated certificate. Our results show that boolean validity indicators, not associated with the authenticated signer identity, are insufficient in practice.
items.title: What You See Is (Not) What You Got: The Human Factor in PDF Signature Verification

items.summary: Modern DRAM chips are vulnerable to read disturbance, which manifests as bitflips in a victim row physically near an aggressor row that is repeatedly activated. State-of-the-art mitigations rely on accurate and exhaustive profiling of the read disturbance threshold (RDT), i.e., the minimum number of aggressor row activations needed to induce the first bitflip. However, RDT changes significantly and unpredictably over time, motivating online profilers that dynamically adjust a mitigation's RDT configuration. RDT profiling is costly for online profilers (e.g., hundreds of seconds for a 16-bank DDR4 module) because 1) measuring a single DRAM row's RDT requires many activations and 2) each DRAM row can have a different RDT, requiring many rows to be profiled. We introduce HARE, an online RDT profiling technique that intentionally exacerbates read disturbance to quickly profile a DRAM module. HARE's key idea is to reduce the timing constraints between consecutive DRAM commands during profiling. Doing so significantly reduces profiling time by 1) directly reducing the execution time of the profiling command sequence and 2) exacerbating read disturbance such that the first bitflip occurs at a smaller activation count than with the conventional RowHammer sequence. From our characterization of 180 real DDR4 DRAM chips from four major DRAM manufacturers, we make three observations. First, HARE measures a DRAM row's RDT 31.2% faster than the RowHammer profiler and a DRAM module's minimum RDT with an average reduction of 21.7%. Second, HARE flips more than 95% of the cells that the RowHammer pattern flips. Third, HARE preserves the RDT ranking of rows well enough such that it can exhaustively reprofile a small set of rows to improve its minimum RDT estimation. Our end-to-end evaluations show that HARE enables significant system performance improvements and outperforms the RowHammer profiler.
items.title: HARE: Fast Read Disturbance Threshold Profiling in Modern DRAM Chips via Reduced Timing Constraints

items.summary: The dissemination of information about known software vulnerabilities occurs online in various ways. Everything from email and development systems to social media are used. Given this variety and a dataset of about 382 thousand online references for about 55 thousand vulnerabilities, the paper demonstrates that the referenced online information sources tend to be mostly dissimilar statistically. The mean cosine similarity between them is only 0.22. Interestingly, the amounts of online references neither increase nor decrease similarity between the online information sources. In contrast, vulnerabilities primarily associated with GitHub and programming language ecosystems tend to have more dissimilar online references than other vulnerabilities. Also vulnerability reports, whether in bug tracking systems or bug bounty platforms, tend to increase dissimilarity. With these empirical results, the paper contributes to the efforts to narrow an enduring knowledge gap related to the online tracking and associated traceability of software vulnerabilities.
items.title: Chinese Whispers About Vulnerabilities

items.summary: We prove that the cyclotomic field $K_{11}=\mathbb{Q}(ζ_{11})$ is unit reducible but not strongly unit reducible. So every nonzero principal fractional ideal of $K_{11}$ has a generator that is a shortest nonzero vector. For $I=h\mathcal{O}_{K_{11}}$, every shortest nonzero vector $α\in I$ satisfies $N_{K_{11}/\mathbb{Q}}(α/h)\in\{1,11\}$. The proof uses Sigrist's Hermite bound for cyclic forms and an averaging identity for cyclotomic units. For principal ideals in $K_{11}$, ideal-SVP and the shortest-generator problem are polynomial-time equivalent.
items.title: Weak Unit Reducibility of the Eleventh Cyclotomic Field

items.summary: We demonstrate a reconfigurable, four-user, full-mesh quantum key distribution network using polarization entanglement, integrated with a software-defined key management system to orchestrate dynamic optical switching and real-time key provisioning for quantum-safe applications.
items.title: Full Mesh Dynamic Four-User Entanglement-based Switched QKD Network Integrated with SD-KMS

items.summary: Data Value Assessment (DVA) plays a critical role in modern data markets by enabling buyers to evaluate how a seller's data would improve model performance before purchase. However, existing DVA approaches require one party to reveal the data or model, exposing participants to privacy leakage, strategic manipulation, and high deployment costs. These limitations motivate a DVA protocol that is secure, reliable, widely applicable, and efficient enough for practical deployment in modern data markets. In this paper, we present SecDVA, the first maliciously secure multi-party computation (MPC) framework for reliable and practical DVA in modern machine learning data markets. SecDVA ensures that neither the seller's data nor the buyer's model and test data are disclosed beyond the final DVA outcome, while remaining robust against malicious behavior. To address the efficiency and applicability challenges of DVA for large models, we use the neural tangent kernel theory to linearize model updates and introduce lightweight mini-batch approximations to significantly reduce computation overhead. We further design a (2+1)-party MPC protocol based on function secret sharing, together with optimized non-linear primitives. In addition, we optimize the underlying MPC backends, the distributed point function, and the distributed comparison function, reducing the number of Advanced Encryption Standard calls to improve efficiency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SecDVA outperforms existing baselines in the plaintext setting and enables DVA for large-scale models in a reasonable time under MPC.
items.title: SecDVA: A Maliciously Secure Multi-Party Framework for Data Value Assessment in Modern Machine Learning Data Markets

items.summary: Building and evaluating security tools for IoT firmware requires targets whose weaknesses are known in ad- vance and can be reproduced in a running device. Two problems remain: (1) firmware collected from real-world products provides realistic software, but hardware dependencies and undocumented defects make it difficult to establish what a security tool should be expected to find; and (2) existing benchmarks typically collect sets of vulnerable or misconfigured firmware images without providing purpose-built vulnerable services with explicit weaknesses that a security analysis tool can target. We present IoTPwnBench, a synthetic, modular benchmark that brings these requirements together. IoTPwnBench contains 716 vulnerable firmware images covering 86 weakness scenarios and 28 CWE classes across 11 device profiles, including industrial controllers, health monitors, and household devices. Each vulnerable image runs a plausible device application with simulated sensors and actuators that generate live readings over its native interfaces while exposing one target weakness mapped to a primary CWE. A documented exploitation payload and observable signal establish the expected behavior independently of the evaluated tool. Every vulnerable image is paired with a corrected twin that preserves the device and service while removing that weakness. Researchers can therefore compare the same target before and after correction to assess detection and false positives for the target weakness. The benchmark produces kernel and filesystem binaries for static inspection and dynamic testing under QEMU. Device profiles and weakness modules remain separate, allowing the same scenario to be reused across device contexts. Vulnerable targets were validated manually, and the open source build workflow regenerates the firmware bit-for-bit.
items.title: IoTPwnBench: A Synthetic Benchmark for IoT Firmware Security Analysis

items.summary: Security decisions about a web page are best made where the page is: in the browser, before anything leaves the machine. We present the Browser Immune System (BIS), a browser extension that screens navigation with a cybersecurity transformer running entirely on the user's GPU, and alias-web, the model that powers it: a 4B-parameter model that starts from the dual-regime cybersecurity transformer (CT0), extends its public release alias3-micro with a context-category sensor, and is quantised to 4 bits and compiled to a 2.44 GB graph for WebGPU. alias-web is the first in-browser realisation of that model's typed decision mode, System 1, with its official pieces: the marker-token mapping, the complete pointer head and the final normalisation that the exported graph omits. It answers a typed security question in about 150 ms on a laptop GPU, and the same weights generate explanations at 10.5 tokens/s on demand. BIS treats the model as an immune system: an innate response, one System 1 question per threat class, runs on every page; an adaptive response, System 2 text, explains a verdict only when the user asks. On BISBENCH-8, eight synthetic sites of which six execute real but harmless malicious behaviour and two are adversarial controls, BIS returns the expected page verdict on 7/8 sites with both controls green and a class-level micro-F1 of 0.71, scans a page in 0.9 to 6.4 s, and gives identical verdicts across samples and across Chrome and Firefox. Single-variable diagnostics trace both benchmark errors to what the model was shown and, with a first pass over eleven real public pages, show that two of the seven questions answer yes on ordinary scripts and login forms: specificity on the real web is the open problem. We report every error, the engineering obstacles between a research checkpoint and a working extension, and what the evidence does not yet support.
